newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech opposition to propose no-confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Czech opposition to propose no-confidence vote.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus called a news conference to make an "important statement" on Friday soon after opposition leader Milos Zeman said he would move for a vote of no confidence in the government.
The prime minister's office would only say that Klaus called the news conference for 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) ON Friday to make an important statement.

Zeman, leader of the main opposition Social Democrats, said he would ask for the no-confidence vote because the ruling coalition's austerity programme announced on Wednesday was a departure from the government's programme announced after 1996 elections.
The Czech crown lost roughly two percent of its value against the mark and dollar less than an hour after Zeman's announcement.

"The crown's fall was partially due to the announcement by Zeman...but it was mostly a foreign reaction. The local market has been hearing this for a while," said Breta Tichanek of ING Bank in Prague.

Klaus's three-party coalition, which holds 100 seats in the 200-seat lower house, agreed on Wednesday to budget cuts, public sector wage freezes, and other measures aimed at stabilising the crown, while acknowledging mistakes were made in their economic policy.
At the same time the finance, industry and trade, education and interior ministers were changed as part of a cabinet shakeup.

Klaus has been under intense pressure over the past two weeks amid a sharp downturn in the economy and heavy pressure on the Czech crown which forced the central bank to float the currency on Tuesday.
Ivan Pilip, part of Klaus's inner circle, was named finance minister to replace Ivan Kocarnik, who many Czechs blamed for the economic problems.

Zeman said the vote of no confidence, which he said would be moved in the lower house session beginning on July 1, was not aimed at forcing early elections but "a real reconstruction, not comic swaps of portfolios".
"What more mistakes must this government make for it to leave voluntarily," Zeman told reporters.
